bib.title: MathPrompter: Mathematical Reasoning using Large Language Models

question: Can zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting be made more accurate and more trustworthy on arithmetic word problems by generating several independent analytical solutions and checking that they agree?
hypothesis: Cross-checking multiple algebraic and Python solutions of a variable-abstracted question, computed on random inputs, gives higher accuracy and confidence than a single zero-shot chain of thought.
contributions: MathPrompter: zero-shot method that abstracts numbers to variables, asks for an algebraic expression and a Python function, verifies them by eval on random values, and takes the consensus
92.5% on MultiArith with a 175B GPT-3, up from 78.7% for Zero-shot-CoT

method.summary: The question is rewritten with numbers replaced by variables (key-value mapping). The LLM is prompted for an algebraic expression and a Python function; both are evaluated with eval() on several random variable assignments, and if they agree the original values are substituted. Steps are repeated N~5 times and the most frequent answer is reported.

datasets.name: MultiArith
datasets.source: Roy & Roth (2016), a subset of the Math World Problem Repository (Koncel-Kedziorski et al. 2016)
datasets.preprocessing: numeric entries replaced by variables A, B, C with a key-value mapping

other.note: exact engine version (e.g. text-davinci-002) not stated for MathPrompter; baseline numbers from Kojima used text-davinci-002
numbers borrowed from Kojima et al. (2022)

inference.samples: steps II and III repeated N~5 times per question; most frequent answer reported; number of random variable assignments not stated beyond 'multiple'
inference.prompting: zero-shot; two instruction prompts (algebraic, Python) applied to the variable-abstracted question; prompt for generating the template Qt is not given

parameters.retry: if no consensus, repeat steps II, III, IV

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: accuracy on MultiArith, not further defined

eval.protocol: baseline numbers borrowed from Kojima et al. (2022); no seeds, runs or significance test reported; single dataset

prompts.text: Write a mathematical equation and generate the answer format starting with 'Answer ='
Write a Python function that returns the answer.

prompts.purpose: Baseline Zero-shot-CoT reasoning and answer extraction

results.claim: MathPrompter reaches 92.5% on MultiArith, versus 78.7% for Zero-shot-CoT.
results.setup: MultiArith, GPT-3 DaVinci 175B, zero-shot, N~5 repeats with consensus; baseline from Kojima et al. with text-davinci-002
results.quote: We were able to improve the accuracy on the MultiArith data from 78.7% →92.5%.

results.claim: Zero-shot-CoT with self-consistency on PaLM 540B scores 89.0, below MathPrompter at 175B.
results.table: Table 1, row Zero-shot-CoT + self consistency (PaLM 540B), column Accuracy

results.claim: Few-Shot-CoT with 8 samples scores 93.0, slightly above MathPrompter.
results.setup: MultiArith, 175B, 8 examples from Wei et al. (2022)
results.table: Table 1, row Few-Shot-CoT (8 samples), column Accuracy

results.claim: Algebraic and Python outputs can agree and still be wrong (candy example: both give 79, correct answer is 54 per the CoT).
results.quote: where both the Algebraic and Pythonic outputs

limits: Authors concede agreement of algebraic and Python outputs does not guarantee correctness (Limitation section).
Evaluated only on MultiArith; further datasets are future work.
Baseline numbers are borrowed from Kojima et al., and the GPT-3 engine version, decoding settings, number of eval values and compute are not stated; no code, no seeds or significance test.
Confidence claim is not quantified; no calibration measurement.
Baseline description of Brown et al. zero-shot in Sec 3.2 is garbled (describes zero-shot class recognition).
